title: Create a `Map<String, Employee>` of department → highest-paid employee (using `Collectors.toMap` with `BinaryOperator.maxBy`).
shortTitle: Create a Map<String, Employee> of department to highest-paid employee

s1_definition.profdef: Using `Collectors.toMap(Employee::getDepartment, e -> e, BinaryOperator.maxBy(comparingDouble(Employee::getSalary)))` keys by department and, on a duplicate department, keeps whichever employee has the higher salary via a comparator-based merge.
s1_definition.analogy: For each department at the National Bank of India, Priya wants to pin up the photo of the top earner. As she goes through the staff, whenever she meets another person from a department she already has, she keeps the one who earns more.
s1_definition.oneliner: `toMap(dept, e->e, BinaryOperator.maxBy(comparing salary))` keeps the highest-paid employee per department.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Using `Collectors.toMap(Employee::getDepartment, e -> e, BinaryOperator.maxBy(comparingDouble(Employee::getSalary)))` keys by department and, on a duplicate department, keeps whichever employee has the higher salary via a comparator-based merge.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** For each department at the National Bank of India, Priya wants to pin up the photo of the top earner. As she goes through the staff, whenever she meets another person from a department she already has, she keeps the one who earns more.

**One line to remember:** `toMap(dept, e->e, BinaryOperator.maxBy(comparing salary))` keeps the highest-paid employee per department.

sections.s2_technical:
The key mapper `Employee::getDepartment` groups by department, and the value mapper `e -> e` keeps the whole employee object as the value. Because many employees share a department, duplicates are expected, so you must supply a merge function. `BinaryOperator.maxBy(Comparator.comparingDouble(Employee::getSalary))` takes the two colliding employees and returns the one with the greater salary.

`BinaryOperator.maxBy` is a convenience that turns any comparator into a two-argument merge that returns the larger element. This is cleaner than writing `(a, b) -> a.getSalary() >= b.getSalary() ? a : b` and it reuses the same comparator you might use elsewhere for sorting. The result is a map from department to the single top earner.

The senior nuance is that this is an alternative to `groupingBy(dept, maxBy(...))`, which would yield `Map<String, Optional<Employee>>`. The toMap-with-maxBy form gives a plain `Map<String, Employee>` with no Optional wrapper, which is often more convenient to consume. Ties are resolved by whichever element the comparator considers not-less, so if tie-breaking matters you extend the comparator.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — A recognition dashboard at the National Bank of India must show, for each department, the single highest-paid employee, with no Optional wrapper to unwrap downstream.

This is exactly what toMap with BinaryOperator maxBy does — it keys by department and keeps the top earner on each collision, producing a clean department-to-employee map.

The code defines a `TopEarnerService.topByDepartment` method and a demo.
sections.s5_journey:
Input: Rajesh IT 1,000,000, Amit IT 800,000, Priya Sales 250,000, Neha Sales 600,000.

Step 1: Rajesh enters under key IT with himself as value.

Step 2: Amit also keys to IT, so the merge runs; maxBy keeps Rajesh because 1,000,000 is greater than 800,000.

Step 3: Priya enters under key Sales.

Step 4: Neha also keys to Sales, so the merge keeps Neha because 600,000 is greater than 250,000.

Step 5: The final map has IT pointing to Rajesh and Sales pointing to Neha.

```
INFO: IT → Rajesh (1000000.0)
INFO: Sales → Neha (600000.0)
```

```
  [Rajesh/IT/1M, Amit/IT/800k, Priya/Sales/250k, Neha/Sales/600k]
    │ toMap(dept, e, maxBy(salary))
    │ IT: max(Rajesh 1M, Amit 800k) = Rajesh
    │ Sales: max(Priya 250k, Neha 600k) = Neha
    ▼
  {IT=Rajesh, Sales=Neha}
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
To find the single highest-paid employee in each department I collect with toMap, using the department as the key and the whole employee object as the value. Because many people share a department, collisions are guaranteed, so I must give a merge function, and the cleanest one is BinaryOperator maxBy wrapping a comparator on salary. When two employees collide on the same department, maxBy hands back the one the comparator considers larger, so the top earner survives.

I prefer this toMap-with-maxBy form on a recognition dashboard at the National Bank of India because it produces a plain map from department to employee, with no Optional wrapper to unwrap. The obvious alternative, groupingBy department with a maxBy downstream, instead gives a map from department to Optional of employee, which is correct but more awkward for consumers.

The senior point I add is that BinaryOperator maxBy is just a convenient adapter that turns any comparator into a two-argument merge returning the larger element, which is far clearer than hand-writing a ternary. Ties are resolved toward whichever element the comparator treats as not-less, so when deterministic tie-breaking matters I simply extend the comparator with a secondary key such as name.
